title: Labels and the table
subtitle: Reading Marlborough and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Labels show the grape, Marlborough GI and vintage, with New Zealand's 85% rules for grape, region and vintage. Some name a sub-region, like Wairau Valley, Awatere Valley or Southern Valleys. Almost all bottles use screw caps; New Zealand led the switch from cork in the early 2000s. Appellation Marlborough Wine is a producer certification for quality and origin.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Marlborough Sauvignon suits green-lipped mussels, a local speciality, oysters, goat's cheese, salads, asparagus and Thai or Vietnamese food with herbs and lime. Pinot Noir suits salmon, duck and lamb. Serve Sauvignon at 7 to 9 degrees and drink within two years; Pinot at 14 to 16.

steps.prompt: Which local shellfish suits Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc?
steps.explanation: Marlborough is a major source of green-lipped mussels.

steps.body: Drink Marlborough Sauvignon young. Its explosive aromas are at their best in the first year or two.

steps.prompt: Most New Zealand wine is sealed with screw caps.
steps.explanation: Yes. New Zealand led the move away from cork.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show the GI and often a sub-region; screw caps are standard
Sauvignon suits green-lipped mussels, goat's cheese and herbs
